Remember God's grace and trust the Messiah (verses 1–3)

People blessed with new birth should remember that they were originally formed in sin.

This remembrance humbles our opinion of ourselves and deepens our appreciation of God's grace.

There is no greater comfort than becoming useful for God's glory.

The more people grow in holiness and do good, the greater their genuine happiness becomes.

Let us reflect seriously upon our guilt.

Such reflection keeps our hearts humble and our consciences awake and sensitive.

It also makes Jesus Christ more precious to us.

Remembering grace strengthens our efforts and prayers for other people's good.

God's salvation outlasts everything earthly (verses 4–8)

Christ's gospel will be proclaimed and made known.

How will we escape if we neglect it?

There is no salvation without righteousness.

Our earthly existence will pass away like smoke.

Our bodies will be laid aside like worn-out clothing.

But people whose happiness rests upon Christ's righteousness and salvation will still enjoy its comfort when time and days themselves have ended.

Clouds may hide the sun for a while, but they cannot stop its course.

Likewise, the believer will continue to enjoy the portion God has promised, while those who mock Christ remain in darkness.

The Redeemer defends and comforts his people (verses 9–16)

Those whom Christ redeemed with his blood and by his power will ultimately be delivered joyfully from every enemy.

If God intends so great a final happiness for us, will he not also give the particular rescues we need on the way?

In this changing world, joy may turn into sorrow almost instantly.

But in the world to come, sorrow will never return.

God's people prayed for a new display of his power.

He answered with the comfort of his grace.

If we feared sinning against God as we ought, we would have much less fear of human disapproval.

Happy is the person who lives in reverent fear of God.

The church of Christ remains secure through the power and Providence of the Almighty.

Jerusalem's suffering and promised release (verses 17–23)

God calls his people to attend to the things that bring everlasting peace.

Jerusalem had provoked him and was made to experience the bitter results.

People who should have comforted her became tormentors themselves.

They lacked the patience needed to keep control of their own souls, and the confidence in God's promises needed to preserve spiritual consolation.

Jerusalem was drunk, not now with the wine of Babylon's idolatry, but with the cup of affliction.

Yet God's cause may appear lost for a time without being lost forever.

He can protect it by awakening the consciences of those opposing it or by defeating their plans.

Oppressors wanted people to submit their souls to human authority—to believe and worship whatever their rulers prescribed.

But violence can obtain only outward and hypocritical conformity.

Consciences cannot be compelled by force.

Freedom announced through Christ's kingdom (verses 1–12)

The gospel declares freedom to those bound by fear.

Let people exhausted and weighed down by the burden of sin come to Jesus Christ for relief.

Shake off the dust of doubts and fears and loosen the chains that bind you.

Our Redeemer did not purchase salvation with silver, gold or any perishable possession.

He paid with his own precious blood.

When we consider how freely this salvation is offered and how much harm sin does even to our earthly peace, we will value Christ's redemption more highly.

Do we seek victory over every sin, remembering that God's glory requires holiness in every person who follows Christ?

The good news is that the Lord Jesus reigns.

Christ himself first announced these tidings.

His ministers now proclaim them.

As they keep themselves clean from the world's corruptions, they become welcome and beautiful messengers to those who receive their message.

Zion's watchmen could scarcely discern evidence of God's favor through the dark cloud of their afflictions.

But now the cloud is removed and they can plainly see the fulfillment of his promise.

Zion's ruined places will rejoice, and the whole world will benefit.

Henry applies this restoration to the salvation offered through Christ.

Babylon is no place for Israelites.

Likewise, anyone enslaved to sin and Satan should make use of the liberty Christ proclaims.

The people should depart quickly and diligently, wasting no time or lingering in captivity.

But they must not depart in fearful, distrustful haste.

Those walking in obedience are under God's special protection.

Faith in that care removes the need for panicked flight.

The Messiah's suffering and exaltation (verses 13–15)

These verses begin a remarkable, detailed and faithful prophecy of the Messiah's office, character and glory.

Henry says its testimony has convinced some of the most stubborn unbelievers.

Christ is Wisdom itself.

The work of redemption reveals the wisdom of God in a mystery.

People who saw Jesus suffering might have thought that no one had ever appeared so miserable.

His sorrow seemed beyond every other sorrow.

Yet God exalted him to the highest honor.

Only Christ's gospel could reveal this saving work as God has now made it known.

Christ shed his blood for sinners once, but its saving power continues.

May those opposing him learn the wisdom of ending their opposition.

May they share in the blood of sprinkling and the baptism of the Holy Spirit, obeying Christ and praising his salvation.

The despised and rejected Messiah (verses 1–3)

Nowhere else in the Old Testament, according to Henry, is it prophesied so plainly and fully that Christ must suffer before entering his glory.

Yet even now many fail to recognize or acknowledge the divine power accompanying this word.

The authentic and supremely important announcement of salvation for sinners through God's Son is neglected.

The humble condition Christ willingly took, and the way he appeared in the world, did not match the ideas many Jews had formed of the Messiah.

They expected a figure arriving with pomp.

Instead, he grew up quietly and almost unnoticed, like a young plant.

He had none of the outward glory people would naturally expect.

His life was not merely humble in social position.

It was also filled with sorrow.

Because he was made sin for us, he endured the sentence to which our sin had exposed us.

Hearts ruled by worldly desires find nothing in Jesus that makes them seek a share in him.

And how many people still despise him through their treatment of his people or reject his teaching and authority!

Christ suffers in our place for our sins (verses 4–9)

Here Scripture describes both Christ's sufferings and their purpose.

Our Lord Jesus suffered for our sins, in our place.

All of us have sinned and fallen short of the glory of God.

Sinners love their own particular sins and cling to the evil paths they have chosen.

Our sins deserve every grief and sorrow, even the most severe judgment.

We are saved from the ruin sin deserves because our sins were laid upon Christ.

This atonement was made for our transgressions.

It is the only way of salvation.

Our sins were the thorns on Christ's head, the nails in his hands and feet, and the spear in his side.

He was given up to death because of our offenses.

Through his suffering, Christ also purchased the Holy Spirit and God's grace for us.

By that grace, the corruption and sinful desires that afflict our souls can be put to death.

If he has taught us to value everything else as loss compared with him, we can endure our far lighter sufferings.

How can we fail to love the One who first loved us?

The willing sacrifice is exalted and justifies sinners (verses 10–12)

Come and see how deeply Christ loved us!

We could never have placed him in our position. He placed himself there willingly.

He took away the sin of the world by taking it upon himself.

He willingly became subject to death, which is the wages of sin for us.

Consider the many graces and glories that follow his humiliation and belong to his exalted state.

Christ does not entrust the ultimate care of his family to anyone else.

God's purposes will certainly be accomplished.

Whatever is undertaken in accordance with his will will prosper.

Christ will see the result in the conversion and salvation of sinners.

Many are justified by him—those for whom he gave his life as a ransom.

We are justified by faith.

In this way God receives the greatest glory, free grace is honored, human pride is humbled and our eternal happiness is secured.

We must know and trust Christ as the One who carried our sins and rescued us from sinking beneath their weight by bearing it himself.

He has defeated the great enemies of his people: sin and Satan, death and hell, the world and the flesh.

Everything the Father intended the Redeemer to obtain will certainly belong to him.

He led captivity captive and received gifts for human beings, to give them gifts.

When we consider the Son of God's sufferings, we should remember the long record of our own transgressions.

Look upon Christ as suffering under the burden of our guilt.

Here is the firm foundation upon which a trembling sinner can rest.

We were purchased by his blood, and our lives display the glory of his grace.

For his people, Christ continually pleads and prevails, destroying the devil's works.

[Isa.53.1-Isa.53.3]
Chapter 53
The person. ( [Isa.53.1-Isa.53.3] Is. 53:1-3) sufferings. ( [Isa.53.4-Isa.53.9] Is. 53:4-9) humiliation, and exaltation of Christ, are minutely described; with the blessings to mankind from his death. ( [Isa.53.10-Isa.53.12] Is. 53:10-12)
Verses 1-3 No where in all the Old Testament is it so plainly and fully prophesied, that Christ ought to suffer, and then to enter into his glory, as in this chapter. But to this day few discern, or will acknowledge, that Divine power which goes with the word. The authentic and most important report of salvation for sinners, through the Son of God, is disregarded. The low condition he submitted to, and his appearance in the world, were not agreeable to the ideas the Jews had formed of the Messiah. It was expected that he should come in pomp; instead of that, he grew up as a plant, silently, and insensibly. He had nothing of the glory which one might have thought to meet with him. His whole life was not only humble as to outward condition, but also sorrowful. Being made sin for us, he underwent the sentence sin had exposed us to. Carnal hearts see nothing in the Lord Jesus to desire an interest in him. Alas! by how many is he still despised in his people, and rejected as to his doctrine and authority!
[Isa.53.4-Isa.53.9]
Verses 4-9 In these verses is an account of the sufferings of Christ; also of the design of his sufferings. It was for our sins, and in our stead, that our Lord Jesus suffered. We have all sinned, and have come short of the glory of God. Sinners have their beloved sin, their own evil way, of which they are fond. Our sins deserve all griefs and sorrows, even the most severe. We are saved from the ruin, to which by sin we become liable, by laying our sins on Christ. This atonement was to be made for our sins. And this is the only way of salvation. Our sins were the thorns in Christ's head, the nails in his hands and feet, the spear in his side. He was delivered to death for our offences. By his sufferings he purchased for us the Spirit and grace of God, to mortify our corruptions, which are the distempers of our souls. We may well endure our lighter sufferings, if He has taught us to esteem all things but loss for him, and to love him who has first loved us.
[Isa.53.10-Isa.53.12]
Verses 10-12 Come, and see how Christ loved us! We could not put him in our stead, but he put himself. Thus he took away the sin of the world, by taking it on himself. He made himself subject to death, which to us is the wages of sin. Observe the graces and glories of his state of exaltation. Christ will not commit the care of his family to any other. God's purposes shall take effect. And whatever is undertaken according to God's pleasure shall prosper. He shall see it accomplished in the conversion and salvation of sinners. There are many whom Christ justifies, even as many as he gave his life a ransom for. By faith we are justified; thus God is most glorified, free grace most advanced, self most abased, and our happiness secured. We must know him, and believe in him, as one that bore our sins, and saved us from sinking under the load, by taking it upon himself. Sin and Satan, death and hell, the world and the flesh, are the strong foes he has vanquished. What God designed for the Redeemer he shall certainly possess. When he led captivity captive, he received gifts for men, that he might give gifts to men. While we survey the sufferings of the Son of God, let us remember our long catalogue of transgressions, and consider him as suffering under the load of our guilt. Here is laid a firm foundation for the trembling sinner to rest his soul upon. We are the purchase of his blood, and the monuments of his grace; for this he continually pleads and prevails, destroying the works of the devil.

The Lord enlarges his church (verses 1–5)

For a long time before Christ came, true religion appeared to have little influence across the world.

But through the preaching of the gospel, multitudes turned from idols to the living God.

This is cause for great rejoicing throughout the church.

Its boundaries are extended.

Its condition on earth remains humble and changeable, like a tent or tabernacle.

But a growing family needs a larger dwelling, and the church should expect its tent to be enlarged.

The more numerous the church becomes, however, the more carefully she must defend herself against false teaching and corruption.

Your Maker is your Husband.

Christ is the Holy One of Israel and the Mediator of the covenant established with God's people under the Old Testament.

For ages he had been called the God of Israel.

Now he will be known as the God of the whole earth.

He cleanses his people from sin and causes every true believer to rejoice in this sacred union.

We cannot admire this mercy enough or adequately value the privilege.

Mercy greater than temporary judgment (verses 6–10)

God is slow to anger and quick to show mercy.

How sweet is the renewed comfort of his mercy when he returns to console his people!

He gathers them not because they deserve it but because he is merciful.

His compassion is great, and his kindness lasts forever.

The wrath is little when compared with the mercy.

His anger lasts a moment, while his loving-kindness is everlasting.

We should neither collapse in despair under present affliction nor give up hoping for relief.

Mountains have been shaken and moved from their places.

But none of God's promises has ever been broken by the events of history.

Mountains and hills may also represent powerful and influential human beings.

The people and created supports in which we place confidence will eventually fail.

But when friends abandon us, God remains faithful.

This promise applies both to the whole church and to individual believers.

God may correct his people for their sins, but he will not finally cast them off.

Let these assurances motivate us to make our calling and election sure.

God's people are taught, protected and justified (verses 11–17)

When God's people are afflicted and storm-tossed, let them hear his words as words of personal consolation, showing that he sees their sorrows and fears.

The church becomes glorious through the knowledge of God.

No teacher can compare with him.

The passage promises the teaching and gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Everyone whom God truly teaches learns to love other people.

Henry sees a special connection with the glorious period that will follow the church's present troubles.

More than outward splendor, holiness is the church's true beauty.

God promises his protection.

There will be neither inward terror nor outward attack able to overturn his purpose.

Soldiers may honor themselves with splendid titles.

But God calls some of them “destroyers made to destroy”, because destruction is their work.

He created them and can direct them to fulfill his own purposes.

The day is coming when he will call wicked people to account for every cruel word (Jude 15).

Security and final victory belong to every faithful servant of the Lord.

Both the righteousness by which believers are justified and the grace through which they are sanctified are gifts from God, resulting from his particular love.

Let us ask him to sanctify our souls and employ us in his service.

[Isa.54.1-Isa.54.5]
Chapter 54
The increase of the church by the conversion of the Jews and Gentiles. ( [Isa.54.1-Isa.54.5] Is. 54:1-5) Its certain deliverance. ( [Isa.54.6-Isa.54.10] Is. 54:6-10) Its triumphant state is described. ( [Isa.54.11-Isa.54.17] Is. 54:11-17)
Verses 1-5 Observe the low state of religion in the world, for a long time before Christianity was brought in. But by preaching the gospel, multitudes were converted from idols to the living God. This is matter of great rejoicing to the church. The bounds of the church were extended. Though its state on earth is but mean and movable, like a tent or tabernacle, it is sometimes a growing state, and must be enlarged as the family increases. But the more numerous the church grows, the more she must fortify herself against errors and corruptions. Thy Maker is thy Husband. Christ is the Holy One of Israel, the Mediator of the covenant made with the Old Testament church. Long he had been called the God of Israel; but now he shall be called the God of the whole earth. And he will cleanse from sin, and cause every true believer to rejoice in this sacred union. We never can enough admire this mercy, or duly value this privilege.
[Isa.54.6-Isa.54.10]
Verses 6-10 As God is slow to anger, so he is swift to show mercy. And how sweet the returns of mercy would be, when God should come and comfort them! He will have mercy on them. God's gathering his people takes rise from his mercy, not any merit of theirs; and it is with great mercies, with everlasting kindness. The wrath is little, the mercies great; the wrath for a moment, the kindness everlasting. We are neither to despond under afflictions, nor to despair of relief. Mountains have been shaken and removed, but the promises of God never were broken by any event. Mountains and hills also signify great men. Creature-confidences shall fail; but when our friends fail us, our God does not. All this is alike applicable to the church at large, and to each believer. God will rebuke and correct his people for sins; but he will not cast them off. Let this encourage us to give the more diligence to make our calling and election sure.
[Isa.54.11-Isa.54.17]
Verses 11-17 Let the people of God, when afflicted and tossed, think they hear God speaking comfortably to them by these words, taking notice of their griefs and fears. The church is all glorious when full of the knowledge of God; for none teaches like him. It is a promise of the teaching and gifts of the Holy Spirit. All that are taught of God are taught to love one another. This seems to relate especially to the glorious times to succeed the tribulations of the church. Holiness, more than any thing, is the beauty of the church. God promises protection. There shall be no fears within; there shall be no fightings without. Military men value themselves on their splendid titles, but God calls them, "Wasters made to destroy," for they make wasting and destruction their business. He created them, therefore he will serve his own designs by them. The day is coming when God will reckon with wicked men for their hard speeches, [Jude.1.15] Jude 1:15. Security and final victory are the heritage of each faithful servant of the Lord. The righteousness by which they are justified, and the grace by which they are sanctified, are the gift of God, and the effect of his special love. Let us beseech him to sanctify our souls, and to employ us in his service.

Come and receive the Savior's gifts without payment (verses 1–5)

Everyone who desires salvation's blessings is welcome to receive them.

In Christ there is enough for everyone and enough for each person.

Those satisfied with worldly things, who feel no need of Christ, experience no spiritual thirst.

They are not troubled about their souls.

But where God gives grace, he also gives a desire for grace.

Where he gives that desire, he will satisfy it.

Come to Jesus Christ!

He is the open fountain and the rock struck to release water.

Come to the holy ordinances, to the streams that make God's city rejoice.

Come to healing water and living water (Revelation 22:17).

Jesus himself used this invitation (John 7:37).

Come and buy: make the gospel's grace your own by personally accepting it.

Come and eat: receive and enjoy the gift.

The world disappoints our expectations.

We hope to find even water there and go thirsty.

But Christ exceeds our expectations.

When we come to him, we find wine and milk.

The gifts offered cannot be assigned an earthly price.

They have already been purchased, at the full cost of Christ's own precious blood (1 Peter 1:19).

Our needs are beyond counting, and we have nothing with which to satisfy them.

If Christ and heaven belong to us, we will remain forever indebted to free grace.

Listen carefully.

Let proud hearts bow.

It is not enough to hear an invitation; accept God's offer.

All the world's wealth and pleasure cannot provide lasting consolation and satisfaction for the soul.

They do not even satisfy our bodily appetites.

Everything is vanity and frustration.

Let the disappointments of earthly life drive us to seek satisfaction in Christ alone.

Only then will our souls find rest.

Listen, and your soul will live.

See how freely happiness is offered!

By the sure mercies of David, Henry understands the Messiah.

All the Savior's mercies are covenant mercies.

He purchased them, God promised them in him, and they are distributed through his hands.

We could not discover the way to living water by ourselves.

Christ is given as Leader and Commander, to show us what to do and to empower us to do it.

Our calling is to obey and follow him.

No one comes to the Father except through him.

He is the Holy One of Israel, faithful to his promises.

God has promised to glorify Christ by giving him the nations as his inheritance.

Seek the Lord while he may be found (verses 6–13)

God now freely offers pardon, peace and lasting happiness.

Seeking him will not be useless while his word calls us and his Spirit works upon our hearts.

But a day is coming when the opportunity will end.

That may happen during a person's earthly life.

It will certainly be over at death and judgment, when the door is closed.

Repentance requires not only a change in conduct, but also a change in the mind.

We must revise our judgments about people and things.

It is not enough to stop outward wrongdoing.

We must struggle against evil thoughts and desires.

To repent is to return to the Lord against whom we rebelled.

If we return, God will multiply pardon, just as we multiplied our offenses.

No one should trifle with that abundant mercy or use it as an excuse to keep sinning.

Human thinking differs sharply from God's thoughts concerning sin, Jesus Christ, holiness, this world and the world to come.

But nowhere does the difference appear more strikingly than in forgiveness.

We may forgive another person yet remain unable to forget the offense.

But when God forgives sin, he no longer remembers it against the sinner.

God's word is effective in Providence and grace just as surely as it governs the natural world.

His holy truth produces changes in human hearts that rain and snow, though essential for the earth, cannot produce.

It never returns to God without accomplishing the purposes for which he sent it.

If we examine the church especially, we will see how much the Lord has accomplished for it and will yet accomplish.

The Jews' return to their homeland pictured greater promised blessings.

Gospel grace transforms the person who receives it.

Rescued from coming wrath, the converted sinner experiences peace of conscience.

Christ's love moves that person to devote life to the Redeemer's service.

Someone once irreverent, quarrelsome, selfish or ruled by sensual pleasures becomes patient, humble, kind and peaceful.

The hope of helping bring about such change should move us to spread the good news of salvation.

And may the Spirit of all truth give us such a view of the fullness, freedom and greatness of God's mercy in Christ that every narrow view of sovereign grace is removed from us.
classic_reading:

Chapter 55
An invitation to receive freely the blessings of the Saviour. ( [Isa.55.1-Isa.55.5] Is. 55:1-5) Gracious offers of pardon and peace. ( [Isa.55.6-Isa.55.13] Is. 55:6-13)
Verses 1-5 All are welcome to the blessings of salvation, to whom those blessings are welcome. In Christ there is enough for all, and enough for each. Those satisfied with the world, that see no need of Christ, do not thirst. They are in no uneasiness about their souls: but where God gives grace, he gives a thirst after it; and where he has given a thirst after it, he will give it. Come to Christ, for he is the Fountain opened, he is the Rock smitten. Come to holy ordinances, to the streams that make glad the city of our God. Come to the healing waters, come to the living waters, Rev. 22:17. Our Saviour referred to this, John 7:37. Come, and buy; make it your own by application of the grace of the gospel to yourselves. Come, and eat; make it still more your own, and enjoy it. The world comes short of our expectations; we promise ourselves, at least, water in it, and we are disappointed; but Christ outdoes our expectations. We come to him, and we find wine and milk. The gifts offered to us are such as no price can be set upon. The things offered are already paid for; for Christ purchased them at the full price of his own blood, I Pet. 1:19. Our wants are beyond number, and we have nothing to supply them; if Christ and heaven are ours, we see ourselves for ever indebted to free grace. Hearken diligently; let the proud heart stoop; not only come, but accept God's offers. All the wealth and pleasure in the world, will not yield solid comfort and content to the soul. Let the disappointments we meet with in the world, help to drive us to Christ, and to seek for satisfaction in him only. Then, and not before, we shall find rest for our souls. Hear, and your soul shall live. On what easy terms is happiness offered us! By the sure mercies of David, we are to understand the Messiah. All his mercies are covenant mercies; they are purchased by him, they are promised in him, and out of his hand they are dispensed to us. We know not how to find the way to the waters, but Christ is given to be a Leader, a Commander, to show us what to do, and enable us to do it. Our business is to obey him, and follow him. There must be not only a change of the way, but a change of the mind. We must alter our judgments about persons and things. But those who place their confidence in God's grace will enter heaven's joy.

His name is holy, and everyone must acknowledge him as the holy God.

Uncontrolled desires and passions make them like a troubled sea.

The Holy Spirit intended this warning for hypocrites in every age.

Fear of suffering and other motives may also suggest, “Spare the rich and powerful.”

If a fast expresses no genuine sorrow for sin and does not lead us to put sin away, it is not a true fast.

The people described here had shown outward signs of sorrow at regular or specially appointed fasts.

Yet they continued indulging pride, greed and hostile passions.

Generosity and mercy are more pleasing to God than empty fasting.

Without them, fasting is vain and hypocritical.

Some people look very humble in God's house while being harsh at home and causing suffering to their own families.

No person's faith can justify that person if it does not work through love.

Still, individuals, families, neighborhoods, churches and whole nations may express genuine repentance by fasting sincerely from right motives and then turning from sin and doing good works.

We must remove the heavy yoke of sin and oppression.

Sin and sorrow can weaken the body and dry up its strength.

By contrast, duties of kindness and charity strengthen and refresh both body and mind.

Good works receive his blessing when they arise from love for God and neighbor and are produced in the heart by the Holy Spirit.

The Sabbath is a sign between God and the people professing to belong to him.

His appointment of it shows his favor toward them.

Their faithful observance of it demonstrates obedience toward him.

Henry calls believers to turn from unnecessary travel and from pursuing their own pleasures on the holy day without the control of conscience.

They must not surrender to sensual pleasures.

On the Sabbath, they should turn from their ordinary businesses and amusements.

In both word and deed, they should mark this day as distinct from the other days of the week.

Even during Old Testament times it was called the Lord's day.

Henry says it is fitting to continue using that name, with the further significance that it is the day of the Lord Jesus Christ (Revelation 1:10).

Many people from distant countries will enter the church.

Christ always welcomes those who come to him.

The gate of mercy remains open day and night.

Everything will be transformed for the better.

No longer will the land hear threats from violent people or the cries of those who suffer violence.

Her walls will represent safety.

Her gates will proclaim praise to God.

The closing images also appear in the description of the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:23; 22:5).

Henry recognizes two possibilities for their fulfillment: a future glorious state of the church on earth, or the triumphant church in heaven.

Only a fulfillment of that magnitude matches the promise.

People who make God their only light will find him their sufficient and everlasting light.

But the God of unlimited power has undertaken it.

Verses 9-14 God will be very gracious. We must begin with his promise, thence all mercies take rise. Many shall be brought into the church, even from far countries. Christ is always ready to receive all who come to him; and the gate of mercy is always open, night and day. All that are about the church shall be made serviceable to it. But those who will not be subject to Christ's golden sceptre, to his word and Spirit, who will not be kept in by the laws and rules of his family, shall be broken in pieces by his iron rod. The peculiar advantages of every nation, and of every description of men, shall join to beautify the church of Christ. We must suppose this to be accomplished in the beauties of holiness, and the graces and comforts of the Spirit, with which gospel ordinances are adorned and enriched. Blessed be his name, the gates of Zion are ever open to returning sinners.
[Isa.60.15-Isa.60.22]
Verses 15-22 We must look for the full accomplishment in times and things, exceeding those of the Old Testament church. The nations and their kings shall lay themselves out for the good of the church. Such a salvation, such a redemption, shall be wrought out for thee, as discovers itself to be the work of the Lord. Every thing shall be changed for the better. In thy land shall no more be heard threats of those that do violence, nor complaints of those that suffer violence. Thy walls shall be means of safety, thy gates shall be written upon with praises to God. In the close of this chapter are images and expressions used in the description of the New Jerusalem, Rev. 21:23; 22:5. Nothing can answer to this but some future glorious state of the church on earth, or the state of the church triumphant in heaven. Those that make God their only light, shall have him their all-sufficient light. And the happiness shall know no change or alloy. No people on earth are all righteous; but there are no mixtures in heaven. They shall be wholly righteous. The spirits of just men shall there be made perfect. The glory of the church shall be to the honour of God. When it shall be finished, it will appear a work of wonder. It may seem too difficult to be brought about, but the God of almighty power has undertaken it. It may seem to be delayed and put off; but the Lord will hasten it in the time appointed by his wisdom, though not in the time prescribed by our folly. Let this hope cheer us under all difficulties, and stir us up to all diligence, that we may have an abundant entrance into this everlasting kingdom of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.
